title: Bacterial Stool Pathogens and Shiga Toxin-Producing E. coli
summary: Choose stool testing by clinical picture, distinguish Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Vibrio, Yersinia and E. coli O157 on the bench, and apply Shiga toxin testing, HUS awareness and the antibiotic warning for STEC.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hits 38–40. Checked against IDSA 2017 (Shane), CDC 2009 STEC recommendations (Gould) and Humphries & Linscott 2015, read as web pages through a page-fetch tool (not as downloaded full text). Correction: Shiga toxin EIA directly on stool is much less sensitive than on enrichment broth (rv-stx-direct-stool). Not taught: Shigella “non-motile, no H2S”, Yersinia “cold enrichment”, Campylobacter “curved” morphology wording, and “never treat with antibiotics” for all STEC (IDSA limits the strong recommendation to O157 and Stx2 strains).

objectives: Decide when stool testing for bacterial pathogens and STEC is indicated.
Distinguish the main enteric bacterial pathogens by culture features.
Apply simultaneous O157 culture and Shiga toxin testing, and explain the HUS and antibiotic warnings.

scenes.title: Bloody stool, no fever
scenes.altText: An invented stool request: a 6-year-old with bloody diarrhea, cramps and no fever. Plates on the bench: MacConkey, Hektoen, a sorbitol-MacConkey plate with colourless colonies, a Campylobacter plate in a microaerobic jar, and a GN broth. Question token: “Which pathogen fits each plate — and what test must not wait for culture?”

cues.text: A six-year-old has bloody diarrhea and cramps, but no fever. The stool arrives in the microbiology lab.
On the bench: MacConkey and Hektoen plates, a sorbitol-MacConkey plate with colourless colonies, a Campylobacter plate in a low-oxygen jar, and an enrichment broth.
Which pathogen fits each plate, and which test must not wait for culture?

props.label: Which pathogen? Which test can’t wait?

scenes.title: Who to test, and with what
scenes.altText: Guideline card (IDSA 2017): test stool for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile and STEC in diarrhea with fever, bloody or mucoid stools, or signs of sepsis; consider STEC in any bloody diarrhea, particularly when fever is absent; the optimal specimen is diarrheal stool (a rectal swab if stool cannot be collected in time). Plate card: MacConkey (MAC), Hektoen (HE), XLD and SS separate lactose fermenters from non-fermenters; normal E. coli ferments lactose.

cues.text: The 2017 infectious-diarrhea guideline says: test for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli when diarrhea comes with fever, bloody or mucoid stool, or sepsis.
Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, STEC, should be considered in any bloody diarrhea, particularly when fever is absent.
The best specimen is diarrheal stool; a rectal swab is acceptable for bacteria if stool cannot be collected in time.
Enteric plates such as MacConkey, Hektoen, XLD and SS separate lactose fermenters, like ordinary E. coli, from non-fermenters.

scenes.title: Telling the pathogens apart
scenes.altText: Five pathogen cards (Humphries & Linscott 2015). Salmonella: lactose non-fermenter with H2S on HE, MAC, XLD, SS; serotyped by somatic (O), flagellar (H) and capsular (Vi) antigens. Shigella: lactose non-fermenter; infectious dose only 10–100 organisms. Campylobacter: microaerobic (~5% O2, 10% CO2) at 42 °C; oxidase-positive; seagull-shaped on stain. Vibrio cholerae: oxidase-positive; yellow colonies on TCBS. Yersinia enterocolitica: CIN agar (also recovers Aeromonas); pinpoint colonies reincubated at 25 °C. STEC O157: does not ferment sorbitol within 24 h → colourless on sorbitol-MacConkey; test in O157 antiserum; most non-O157 STEC ferment sorbitol.

cues.text: Salmonella does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide on Hektoen, MacConkey, XLD and SS agar. It is serotyped by its O, H and Vi antigens.
Shigella also does not ferment lactose, and as few as 10 to 100 organisms can cause infection.
Campylobacter needs a low-oxygen atmosphere at 42 degrees. It is oxidase-positive and looks seagull-shaped on stain.
Vibrio cholerae is oxidase-positive and grows as yellow colonies on TCBS. Yersinia is recovered on CIN agar, with small colonies reincubated at 25 degrees.

E. coli O157 does not ferment sorbitol within 24 hours, so it forms colourless colonies on sorbitol-MacConkey; confirm with O157 antiserum. But most non-O157 STEC do ferment sorbitol, so the plate misses them.

props.title: Vibrio · Yersinia
lines: V. cholerae: oxidase +, yellow on TCBS

scenes.title: Shiga toxin testing cannot wait
scenes.altText: Testing card: culture for O157 AND test for Shiga toxin (or stx genes) at the same time — non-O157 STEC are found only by toxin or gene assays (IDSA 2017; CDC 2009). Shiga toxin immunoassays are performed on overnight enrichment broth; on raw stool directly they are much less sensitive (~70%). HUS card: thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia and renal failure; Shiga toxin 2 strains carry a higher risk; O157 infections carry the highest. Treatment card: avoid antibiotics for STEC O157 and other Shiga toxin 2-producing STEC — they may increase HUS risk. Public health card: forward O157 isolates and toxin-positive broths to the public health laboratory; culture CIDT-positive specimens so isolates are available. Back to the hook: colourless SMAC colonies + bloody stool without fever → STEC O157 likely; run Shiga toxin testing now.

cues.text: Culture for O157 and test for Shiga toxin or its genes at the same time. Non-O157 STEC are only found by toxin or gene tests.
Toxin immunoassays work best on an overnight enrichment broth; run directly on stool, sensitivity falls to about 70 percent. Gene tests are an alternative.
The danger is hemolytic uremic syndrome: low platelets, hemolytic anemia and kidney failure. Strains making Shiga toxin 2 carry a higher risk.
Antibiotics should be avoided for O157 and other Shiga toxin 2 strains, because they may increase the risk of HUS. Forward isolates and toxin-positive broths to the public health laboratory.
Back to the child: colourless sorbitol-MacConkey colonies and bloody stool without fever point to STEC O157, and the Shiga toxin test should run now.

props.label: Send isolates + Stx+ broths to public health
Colourless SMAC + bloody, afebrile → STEC: test toxin now

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A negative sorbitol-MacConkey culture rules out STEC” (✓ most non-O157 STEC ferment sorbitol; test for Shiga toxin or stx genes); “Run the Shiga toxin EIA on raw stool — it’s faster” (✓ broth enrichment is more sensitive; direct stool ~70%); “Give antibiotics to shorten STEC illness” (✓ avoid in O157/Stx2 — may increase HUS risk).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative sorbitol-MacConkey culture rules out STEC. No: most non-O157 strains ferment sorbitol. Test for Shiga toxin or its genes.
Trap two: run the toxin immunoassay straight on stool because it is faster. Direct stool testing is much less sensitive; use enrichment broth or a gene test.
Trap three: give antibiotics to shorten STEC illness. No: for O157 and Shiga toxin 2 strains, antibiotics may increase the risk of HUS.

props.title: ✗ “Stx EIA on raw stool is best.”

scenes.title: Sorbitol-shy, toxin-loud
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “O157 is sorbitol-shy but toxin-loud — and antibiotics make it louder.” Tokens: Colourless on SMAC · Test the toxin · No antibiotics. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: O157 is sorbitol-shy but toxin-loud, and antibiotics make it louder. Colourless on sorbitol-MacConkey, always test for the toxin, and avoid antibiotics.
Where it breaks: most non-O157 strains are not sorbitol-shy; some O157 variants ferment sorbitol; and antibiotic advice for strains without Shiga toxin 2 is debated.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Salmonella LNF + H2S · Shigella LNF, dose 10–100 · Campylobacter 42 °C microaerobic, oxidase + · V. cholerae yellow TCBS · Yersinia CIN”, “O157 sorbitol − on SMAC · always test Shiga toxin (broth EIA or NAAT) · avoid antibiotics · forward isolates”.

cues.text: Bloody diarrhea, especially without fever, needs Shiga toxin testing alongside culture, because sorbitol-MacConkey finds only O157 and antibiotics may raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome.

props.label: Salmonella LNF + H2S · Shigella LNF · Campy 42 °C micro · Vibrio TCBS · Yersinia CIN
O157 sorbitol − · test Shiga toxin (broth EIA/NAAT) · no antibiotics · send isolates

explanation.what: Plain language: several bacteria cause diarrhea, and the lab sorts them out with special plates and tests; one group, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, can damage blood and kidneys, so its toxin is tested for quickly. Scientific terms: lactose fermentation, H2S, MacConkey, Hektoen, XLD, SS, sorbitol-MacConkey (SMAC), TCBS, CIN agar, microaerobic, Shiga toxin (Stx1, Stx2), STEC, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), culture-independent diagnostic test (CIDT).
explanation.why: Pathogens differ in carbohydrate fermentation, H2S production and growth requirements, which selective/differential media exploit. E. coli O157 does not ferment sorbitol within 24 h, but most non-O157 STEC do, so only toxin or gene detection finds all STEC. Shiga toxin 2 strains carry the greatest HUS risk, and antibiotics might increase it.
explanation.measure: IDSA 2017: test for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile and STEC with fever, bloody/mucoid stool or sepsis; O157 by culture and non-O157 by Shiga toxin/genomic assays; avoid antibiotics for O157 and Stx2 STEC. Humphries 2015: Salmonella LNF with H2S; Shigella dose 10–100; Campylobacter 42 °C microaerobic, oxidase +; V. cholerae yellow on TCBS; Yersinia CIN, 25 °C; Stx EIA on enrichment broth, direct stool ~70% sensitivity. CDC 2009: simultaneous culture and EIA; forward isolates and Stx-positive broths; HUS = thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, renal failure.
explanation.differs: O157 (sorbitol-negative, culture on SMAC) vs non-O157 STEC (usually sorbitol-positive; toxin/gene tests); broth-enriched vs direct stool Stx EIA; Salmonella (H2S +) vs Shigella (LNF, low dose); oxidase-positive Campylobacter and Vibrio.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: SMAC and O157, why Shiga toxin testing must accompany culture, HUS triad, antibiotics contraindicated, and media/conditions for Campylobacter, Vibrio and Yersinia.

questions.stem: A stool from a child with bloody diarrhea grows only sorbitol-fermenting (pink) E. coli on sorbitol-MacConkey. What is the best next step?

options.text: Test for Shiga toxin or stx genes (e.g., EIA on enrichment broth or NAAT)
options.rationale: Correct. Most non-O157 STEC ferment sorbitol, so only toxin or gene detection finds them.
Incorrect. SMAC screens only for sorbitol-negative O157.

options.text: Test the pink colonies with O157 antiserum
options.rationale: Incorrect. O157 antiserum is applied to sorbitol-nonfermenting colonies.
Incorrect. Antibiotics are avoided for STEC O157 and Stx2 strains because they may increase HUS risk.

questions.stem: A small, oxidase-positive, seagull-shaped gram-negative rod grows from stool incubated at 42 °C in a microaerobic atmosphere. What is it most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Campylobacter is recovered microaerobically at 42 °C and is oxidase-positive.
Incorrect. Shigella is a lactose non-fermenter recovered on enteric media such as MAC, HE, XLD and SS, not the 42 °C microaerobic Campylobacter plate.
Incorrect. Salmonella is a lactose non-fermenter that produces H2S on enteric media.
Incorrect. Yersinia is recovered on CIN agar, with reincubation at 25 °C, not microaerobically at 42 °C.

questions.stem: Which triad defines hemolytic uremic syndrome after STEC infection?

options.text: Thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia and renal failure
options.rationale: Correct. This is the HUS triad described by CDC.
Incorrect. These describe other syndromes, such as toxic shock.
Incorrect. These are features of liver disease.
Incorrect. These are not features of HUS.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says to detect Shiga toxin directly in stool by EIA. Humphries 2015 and CDC 2009 recommend EIA on enrichment broth; direct stool EIA has much lower sensitivity (~70%). NAAT for stx genes on stool is acceptable. See register flag rv-stx-direct-stool.
